e.meaning: twisted, coiled; the sea monster of the Bible
e.etymology: From Hebrew livyatan, the coiled sea monster of Job, Psalms and Isaiah, from a root meaning to twist. In English the word came to mean anything of enormous size.

assoc.t: leviathan, the Bible's sea monster and a word for a giant
Leviathan, Thomas Hobbes's 1651 book on government

e.note: In the Bible Leviathan is a sea monster, often read as a symbol of chaos or evil.

e.etymology: The English word for courageous, borrowed from French brave and Italian bravo. It is a recent American virtue name.
A variant of Melinda in use since the 1700s. Melinda was coined in English by joining Mel-, as in Melissa and Melanie, to the -inda ending of Belinda and Lucinda.
An American spelling of Stephen that follows the sound of Stefan and French Stéphane. All come from Greek stephanos, crown or garland.
namesakes: Stephon Gilmore (NFL cornerback, 2019 Defensive Player of the Year)

e.etymology: A short form of Zachary and Zachariah, from Hebrew Zekharyah, Yahweh has remembered.
namesakes: Zach Galifianakis (comedian, star of The Hangover)

e.etymology: In Persian, sima means face or countenance. In Jewish use it comes from Aramaic sima, treasure. In India the same name, more often spelled Seema, is from Sanskrit sima, boundary.
From Arabic Safiyya, pure, from safi, clear or pure. Safiyya bint Huyayy was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad.
A form of the Hebrew name Nesya, from nes, miracle, and Yah, a short form of God's name.
A Sikh name joining gur, the Guru, with baaz, falcon, a Persian loanword in Punjabi. The falcon is the bird linked with Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru.
A feminine form of Adrian, from Latin Hadria, the town in northern Italy that also named the Adriatic Sea. In Catalan, Adrià is a masculine form.
namesakes: Adria Arjona (actress in Andor and Hit Man)

e.etymology: A modern American name that extends Jana and Janae, forms of Jane, with the -aya ending of Amaya and Anaya. Jane goes back to Hebrew Yohanan, God is gracious.
From Sanskrit yashas, fame or glory. It is used on its own and as the first part of names such as Yashwant and Yashpal.
A short form of the Greek name Athanasios, immortal, from a-, not, and thanatos, death. In English it may also have arisen from Nathan, by hearing my Nathan as mine Athan.

assoc.t: athan or adhan, the Islamic call to prayer

e.etymology: A spelling of Aleida, a Dutch and Spanish short form of Adelheid, the Germanic name behind Adelaide, from adal, noble, and heid, kind or sort.
A respelling of Eliza, a short form of Elizabeth that has stood on its own since the 1700s. Elizabeth comes from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
A short form of surnames and first names such as Whitney, Whitman and Whitaker, most of which begin with Old English hwit, white.

assoc.t: whit, an old word for a tiny bit, as in not a whit

e.etymology: The Arabic elative of sa'id, happy or lucky, so it means happier or most fortunate. It is related to Saad and Saeed.
e.note: Sounds like Assad, the surname of Syria's former rulers, though that name comes from a different Arabic word.

e.etymology: From Persian sitara, star, a word that passed into Urdu and Hindi and shares an ancient root with English star.
From Chinese mulan, the lily magnolia. Hua Mulan is the heroine of a ballad more than 1,400 years old about a daughter who takes her father's place in the army.
namesakes: Hua Mulan (legendary Chinese woman warrior, heroine of Disney's Mulan)

e.etymology: The French and German form of Bridget, from Irish Brighid, exalted one, the name of a Celtic goddess and of Saint Brigid of Kildare.
namesakes: Brigitte Bardot (French film star of the 1950s and 1960s)
Brigitte Nielsen (Danish actress in Rocky IV)

e.etymology: From the River Afton in Ayrshire, Scotland, which Robert Burns praised in his song Sweet Afton: Flow gently, sweet Afton. It later came into use as a first name in the US.

assoc.t: William Afton, villain of Five Nights at Freddy's
Sweet Afton, Robert Burns's song about the river

e.note: Kids who know Five Nights at Freddy's will link Afton to William Afton, the game's child-killing villain.

e.etymology: A form of Demetrius, from Greek Demetrios, belonging to Demeter, the goddess of grain and the harvest. Her name is read as earth mother.
A modern name, read as a contraction of Viviana or a blend of Vivian and Anna. Viana and Vianna are also Portuguese place names and surnames.
A surname turned first name, also read as a bold spelling of the word striker. In the US it is known from the Army's Stryker armored vehicle and the Stryker medical company.

assoc.t: Stryker, the US Army's eight-wheeled armored vehicle

e.etymology: A modern Indian name, more often spelled Saanvi, popularly taken as a name of the goddess Lakshmi. Its Sanskrit derivation is unclear.
From Sanskrit arohi, ascending, built on aroha, a rise or climb. In Indian classical music the aroha is the ascending run of notes in a raga.
From Greek aella, whirlwind or storm wind. In Greek myth Aella was an Amazon, the first to attack Heracles when he came for Hippolyta's girdle.
e.note: Aella is also the pen name of an American online writer on sex research who is a former sex worker.

e.etymology: A modern American elaboration of Amir, Arabic for prince or commander, with the -ion ending of Darion and Amarion.
A spelling of Alice that takes the French-style sound of Elise. Alice comes through Old French Aalis from the Germanic name Adalheidis, noble kind.
Originally a nickname from the English word buck, a male deer or goat, given to a spirited young man. It became a surname and then a cowboy-flavored American first name.
namesakes: Buck Owens (country star and co-host of Hee Haw)
Buck (the dog in Jack London's The Call of the Wild)

e.etymology: A short form of Alexis and an English spelling of Russian Aleksei, both from Greek alexein, to defend. The same root gives Alexander.
namesakes: Alexi Lalas (US soccer star and television analyst)
